question: Is the extra health worth the extra cost?

sanders2016.cite: Sanders et al. (2016). Recommendations for conduct, methodological practices, and reporting of cost-effectiveness analyses: Second Panel on Cost-Effectiveness in Health and Medicine. JAMA 316(10): 1093–1103.
sanders2016.checked: every quote read word for word in the vault's text copy of the published version deposited in White Rose Research Online (library No. 291) on 20 Nov 2026; definitions are from the article's glossary of key terms and are cited by term, recommendations by number; in-text reference numbers are left out

steps.title: Pick the comparison
steps.text: Name the intervention, what it is compared with, for whom, and from whose point of view costs are counted.

quotes.text: All cost-effectiveness analyses should report 2 reference case analyses: one based on a health care sector perspective and another based on a societal perspective.

steps.title: Count the costs
steps.text: Add up the costs of each alternative over the time horizon, bringing future costs and health back to present values.

quotes.text: The process of converting future dollars and future health outcomes to their present values.

steps.title: Count the health
steps.text: Measure health gained in quality-adjusted life years: each year weighted by its quality of life, from 0 (as bad as death) to 1 (full health).

quotes.text: A measure of health outcome that assigns a weight to each period (ranging from 0 to 1), corresponding to the health-related quality of life during that period

steps.title: Divide the differences
steps.text: The extra cost divided by the extra health is the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio: the price of one more QALY.

quotes.text: The ratio of the difference in costs between 2 alternatives to the difference in effectiveness between the same 2 alternatives.

steps.title: Shake the assumptions
steps.text: Vary the uncertain inputs and show how the answer moves. A ratio that flips with one price is not a firm answer.

quotes.text: Analysts should be transparent about how they have conducted the analyses, and convey how the results change with alternative assumptions.

exercise.title: Find the price of a QALY
exercise.intro: A new treatment costs more than usual care and gives more health. Move its price and the health gain, then set what a decision maker is willing to pay per QALY, and see whether it passes.

quote.text: The ratio of the difference in costs between 2 alternatives to the difference in effectiveness between the same 2 alternatives.

exercise.data_label: Example data, made up for this exercise: usual care costs 10 000 and gives 5.0 QALYs per patient; the willingness to pay is yours to choose, not any agency's threshold.

limits: Sanders et al. (2016) write for the United States (costs in dollars); the NICE example on the card is not checked here and no real threshold is given.
Decision models (decision trees, Markov models) and probabilistic sensitivity analysis are not shown.
